slides.title: The Core Problem
slides.lead:
A single server gives a web application only one path for requests, so its failure stops everything
Cloud architectures fix this by placing multiple servers behind a traffic distributor

points.text: Single point of failure: one component whose failure stops the entire application
Hardware failure, an operating-system patch, or a crash removes the only server
Traffic above the server's capacity slows or drops requests, since no second server exists
A bigger server raises capacity but never removes the single point of failure

slides.notes: Start by stating that one server means one failure point, linking it to the earlier horizontal-scaling idea. Use the ticket-counter analogy to make the outage concrete before introducing load balancing. Interviewers often ask what a single point of failure means — this slide answers that.

slides.label: Analogy: one ticket counter
slides.title: The Core Problem
slides.notes:
TR analogy: A railway station with only one ticket counter forces every passenger to wait once that counter closes for a break — exactly as a single server failing removes the only route available for every user's request.

"Start by stating that one server means one failure point, linking it to the earlier horizontal-scaling idea. Use the ticket-counter analogy to make the outage concrete before introducing load balancing. Interviewers often ask what a single point of failure means — this slide answers that."

slides.title: Load Balancer Role
slides.lead: A load balancer is a component that receives all incoming requests and distributes them across multiple backend servers, so no single server is overloaded or becomes a single point of failure
slides.notes: Explain the load balancer as the layer between users and servers, deciding where each request goes. Note that this is the exact service used later in the practical, reachable from the EC2 console. A common interview question asks why users cannot get a fixed server address directly — this mechanism is the answer.

slides.title: Load Balancer Role

points.text: Identical servers behind the load balancer let one fail without downtime
Adding or removing backend servers changes capacity without changing application code
AWS offers this as Elastic Load Balancing, set up from the EC2 console

slides.notes: Explain the load balancer as the layer between users and servers, deciding where each request goes. Note that this is the exact service used later in the practical, reachable from the EC2 console. A common interview question asks why users cannot get a fixed server address directly — this mechanism is the answer.

slides.title: Load Balancer Role

points.text: An Application Load Balancer is billed hourly plus traffic processed
Choosing a load balancer type is also a cost decision

slides.notes: Explain the load balancer as the layer between users and servers, deciding where each request goes. Note that this is the exact service used later in the practical, reachable from the EC2 console. A common interview question asks why users cannot get a fixed server address directly — this mechanism is the answer.

slides.title: Why It Exists
slides.lead: Removing the single point of failure is not the only benefit; the same routing that avoids failed servers also lets capacity grow by adding more servers

points.text: Availability: traffic keeps reaching healthy servers during instance failure or patching
Scalability: new servers join the load balancer as demand grows, with no downtime
Horizontal scaling works safely only when users reach the load balancer, not a fixed server address
Extra backend servers for availability add compute cost, a trade-off covered later

slides.notes: Stress that availability and scalability both come from rerouting traffic, applied to failure versus growth. Mention that more servers mean more cost, without a pricing discussion. Note that distributing traffic needs a defined method, which the next section covers.

slides.title: Two Classification Axes
slides.lead:
Load balancers are classified in two ways: by the OSI layer they work at, and by who can reach them
Both choices change routing intelligence, speed, and exposure

points.text: Layer axis: Layer 4 balancers route by IP and port; Layer 7 balancers read HTTP content
Internet-facing: has a public IP and accepts requests from users on the internet
Internal: has only a private IP and routes traffic between services inside the private network

slides.notes: Set up both axes before going deep into either one. Say plainly: layer decides how smart the routing is, exposure decides who can send traffic. Mention this map will be filled in across the next three slides.

slides.title: Two Classification Axes
slides.lead: A real deployment picks one from each axis, like an internet-facing Layer 7 balancer
slides.notes: Set up both axes before going deep into either one. Say plainly: layer decides how smart the routing is, exposure decides who can send traffic. Mention this map will be filled in across the next three slides.

slides.title: Balancer Comparison
slides.lead:
Layer 4 balancers forward packets using only transport headers, while Layer 7 balancers terminate the connection and read the full HTTP request
AWS calls these Network Load Balancer (NLB) and Application Load Balancer (ALB)
slides.notes: Layer 4 is faster since it never opens the packet; Layer 7 is smarter since it inspects HTTP data. Note the AWS names, as they appear on the console. Interview hook: ask when NLB beats ALB for raw TCP/UDP speed and preserving client IP.

slides.title: Balancer Comparison

cells: Reads full HTTP request and response
Rule-based routing to different pools by path or host

slides.notes: Layer 4 is faster since it never opens the packet; Layer 7 is smarter since it inspects HTTP data. Note the AWS names, as they appear on the console. Interview hook: ask when NLB beats ALB for raw TCP/UDP speed and preserving client IP.

slides.title: Who Can Reach It
slides.lead: Load balancers are also classified by exposure: internet-facing balancers get a public IP and accept internet traffic, while internal balancers get only a private IP, reachable within their VPC

points.text: Internal balancers connect internal tiers, like an application calling a backend service
Internal balancers shrink the attack surface since no public route exists
Exposure type and layer type are independent; both can be Layer 4 or Layer 7

slides.notes: Stress that exposure is separate from layer, not a variant of it. Use public reception versus staff-only corridor as the everyday phrasing. Exam hook: ask why making a database-facing balancer internal-only is good security practice.

slides.label: Analogy: reception desk and staff corridors
slides.title: Who Can Reach It
slides.notes:
TR analogy: An office building has a public reception desk anyone off the street can walk into, and separate staff-only corridors reachable only by employees already inside — just as an internet-facing balancer accepts any public visitor while an internal balancer accepts only traffic that already originates inside the VPC.

"Stress that exposure is separate from layer, not a variant of it. Use public reception versus staff-only corridor as the everyday phrasing. Exam hook: ask why making a database-facing balancer internal-only is good security practice."

slides.title: Combining Both Axes
slides.lead: A typical architecture places an internet-facing Layer 7 balancer in front of user traffic and an internal Layer 4 or 7 balancer between services, matching intelligence to each hop
slides.notes: Tie both axes together with one concrete architecture to make the choice practical. Point to the EC2 console's load balancer creation screen as where this setting lives. Note that an algorithm still decides which server gets each request once traffic reaches the right balancer.

slides.title: Combining Both Axes

points.text: AWS provides an ALB for Layer 7 traffic and an NLB for Layer 4
The internet-facing or internal scheme is set once, in the EC2 console
Public websites typically use an internet-facing ALB; internal calls use an NLB or ALB
An ALB receives traffic through a listener (a protocol and port)
And forwards it to a target group, a named set of backend servers that share a health check

slides.notes: Tie both axes together with one concrete architecture to make the choice practical. Point to the EC2 console's load balancer creation screen as where this setting lives. Note that an algorithm still decides which server gets each request once traffic reaches the right balancer.

slides.label: Four Approaches Compared
slides.notes: "Frame this as the rulebook a load balancer consults for every request. Stress that none of the four is universally best; each suits a different traffic shape. Interviewers may ask which algorithm fits a scenario, so link each name to its trigger."

props.title: Four Approaches Compared
lines: A load balancer needs a rule, called an algorithm, to pick a healthy target for each request
Algorithms fall into two types: static algorithms follow fixed rules and ignore server load, while dynamic algorithms check live server state before deciding

slides.title: Four Approaches Compared
slides.notes: "Frame this as the rulebook a load balancer consults for every request. Stress that none of the four is universally best; each suits a different traffic shape. Interviewers may ask which algorithm fits a scenario, so link each name to its trigger."
slides.lead: Many variations exist, but four are used most widely

points.text: Round robin (static): cycles through targets in fixed order, assuming equal capacity
Least connections (dynamic): picks the target with the fewest active connections
IP hash (static): maps a client’s IP address to the same target, as long as the server pool stays the same
Weighted distribution (static or dynamic): adds capacity weights to round robin or least connections
So stronger targets get more traffic

slides.title: Static Capacity Bias
slides.notes: "Explain smoothing via the running-total idea so the order isn't clumped — a common exam trip-up. Note that weights are manual and planned, unlike least connections which reacts automatically. Mention AWS target group weight field as the real-world example."
slides.lead: Plain round robin treats all targets equally, which fails when server capacity differs

slides.title: Static Capacity Bias
slides.notes: "Explain smoothing via the running-total idea so the order isn't clumped — a common exam trip-up. Note that weights are manual and planned, unlike least connections which reacts automatically. Mention AWS target group weight field as the real-world example."
slides.lead: Weighted distribution gives stronger targets a proportionally larger share of the rotation

slides.title: Static Capacity Bias
slides.notes: "Explain smoothing via the running-total idea so the order isn't clumped — a common exam trip-up. Note that weights are manual and planned, unlike least connections which reacts automatically. Mention AWS target group weight field as the real-world example."

points.text: Smooth weighted round robin increases each target's running total by its weight, avoiding bursts
A 3:1 weight ratio averages three requests to one target per other request
Weights are set once from known capacity, not changed automatically with load

slides.title: Static Capacity Bias
slides.notes: "Explain smoothing via the running-total idea so the order isn't clumped — a common exam trip-up. Note that weights are manual and planned, unlike least connections which reacts automatically. Mention AWS target group weight field as the real-world example."

points.text: On AWS ALB, the default routing algorithm within a target group is round robin
Weighted target groups can be configured in listener rules
To distribute traffic between target groups (for example, 90:10)
These are two different mechanisms

slides.title: Dynamic Load Tracking
slides.notes: "Emphasise that the counter is live, updating on every request start and finish, unlike a fixed weight. Use an upload example to show why duration matters more than request count. Remember the AWS term, least outstanding requests, for interviews."
slides.lead: Round robin and weighting follow a fixed plan, but least connections reacts continuously, sending each new request to whichever target is least busy

slides.title: Dynamic Load Tracking
slides.notes: "Emphasise that the counter is live, updating on every request start and finish, unlike a fixed weight. Use an upload example to show why duration matters more than request count. Remember the AWS term, least outstanding requests, for interviews."

points.text: A per-target counter rises when a request starts and falls on completion
Long-lived connections let least connections outperform round robin under uneven request durations
AWS ALB’s least outstanding requests option, selected in the target group settings
Counts in-flight requests, not raw connections
No manual tuning is needed; counts adjust as servers speed up or slow down

slides.label: Client To Server Mapping
slides.notes: "Introduce the session-affinity problem before naming IP hash. Flag the reshuffle risk when targets change, since interviewers often ask about it. Mention Network Load Balancer's flow hashing as the transport-layer equivalent."

props.title: Client To Server Mapping
lines: Some applications keep client state only on the server that first handled a request, so later requests must return there
IP hash hashes the client's source IP to pick a fixed target

slides.title: Client To Server Mapping
slides.notes: "Introduce the session-affinity problem before naming IP hash. Flag the reshuffle risk when targets change, since interviewers often ask about it. Mention Network Load Balancer's flow hashing as the transport-layer equivalent."

points.text: Adding or removing a target reshuffles mapping, redirecting many clients at once
Clients sharing one corporate or mobile-network gateway IP can overload a single target disproportionately
AWS has no setting named IP hash: ALB uses cookie-based stickiness; NLB offers source-IP stickiness
IP hash avoids shared session stores, unlike server-side replication methods

slides.label: Analogy: exam halls by roll number
slides.title: Client To Server Mapping
slides.notes:
TR analogy: In an exam, each student’s hall is decided by their roll number (for example, the last digit decides the hall), so the same student always goes to the same hall. In the same way, IP hash uses the client’s IP address to always route that client to the same backend server.

"Introduce the session-affinity problem before naming IP hash. Flag the reshuffle risk when targets change, since interviewers often ask about it. Mention Network Load Balancer's flow hashing as the transport-layer equivalent."

slides.label: Section Topic Map

props.title: Section Topic Map
lines: A load balancer must know which backends are actually working, and decide how a user's follow-up requests are handled across multiple servers

slides.notes: "Present these three as one connected story: detect failure, remove backend safely, then handle returning users. Note this builds on the distribution algorithms already covered. Exam angle: expect a question distinguishing health checks from session stickiness."

slides.label: How Checks Work

props.title: How Checks Work
props.lead: A health check works like a repeated vitals check: the load balancer sends a test request and reads the reply, confirming the application is actually responding, not just running

points.text: Interval: sets how often the check repeats; the ALB default is every 30 seconds
Timeout: longest time the backend is given to reply before a miss
Healthy threshold: consecutive passes needed before traffic resumes to a backend
Unhealthy threshold: consecutive failures needed before traffic stops to a backend

slides.notes: Stress that a server can be powered on yet still fail a health check if the application crashes while the OS keeps running. Use 'repeated vitals check' before naming the thresholds. Interview hook: ask what happens if the interval is too long or too short, since that trades detection speed against false alarms.

slides.label: Analogy: a repeated vitals check
slides.title: How Checks Work
slides.notes:
TR analogy: A doctor does not assume a patient is fine just because they are breathing; a short, repeated vitals check confirms the body is actually functioning — just as a health check confirms the server is actually serving requests correctly, not merely running.

Stress that a server can be powered on yet still fail a health check if the application crashes while the OS keeps running. Use 'repeated vitals check' before naming the thresholds. Interview hook: ask what happens if the interval is too long or too short, since that trades detection speed against false alarms.

slides.label: Removing A Backend Safely

props.title: Removing A Backend Safely
lines: Instant removal would cut off in-flight requests
Draining gives the backend a grace period, the deregistration delay, to finish current work before leaving rotation

slides.notes: "Draining is the polite way to retire a server, unlike yanking it out mid-request. It also runs during planned scale-down, not just after a failed health check. Exam angle: draining exists to avoid breaking in-flight requests."

slides.title: Removing A Backend Safely

points.text: An unhealthy backend stops getting new traffic at once
When it is deregistered (for example, replaced by Auto Scaling), draining lets its in-flight requests finish
New requests stop reaching the backend as soon as deregistration starts (manual removal, scale-in or a deployment)

slides.notes: "Draining is the polite way to retire a server, unlike yanking it out mid-request. It also runs during planned scale-down, not just after a failed health check. Exam angle: draining exists to avoid breaking in-flight requests."

slides.title: Removing A Backend Safely

points.text: In-progress requests on that backend complete normally during the grace period
The deregistration delay is a target group setting; the AWS default is 300 seconds
Once the delay expires, any remaining connections are closed

slides.notes: "Draining is the polite way to retire a server, unlike yanking it out mid-request. It also runs during planned scale-down, not just after a failed health check. Exam angle: draining exists to avoid breaking in-flight requests."

slides.title: Two Session Approaches
slides.lead: HTTP is stateless by default, so a load balancer must decide whether a returning user must land on the same backend, or whether any backend can serve them equally well
slides.notes: "Link this to draining: a sticky user on a draining backend forces a remap. Stateless design is preferred since it lets instances be added or removed freely. Interview hook: stateless design scales better because it removes server-affinity bottlenecks."

slides.title: Two Session Approaches

cells: A cookie set by the load balancer binds a user to one backend for the session duration
Breaks if that backend drains or fails, and skews load unevenly
Session data lives outside the server, so any healthy backend can answer any request
Needs an external store, but removal and scaling stay simple

slides.notes: "Link this to draining: a sticky user on a draining backend forces a remap. Stateless design is preferred since it lets instances be added or removed freely. Interview hook: stateless design scales better because it removes server-affinity bottlenecks."

slides.title: Routing And Delivery
slides.notes: Frame this as traffic steering at a wider scale than load balancing. DNS decides which region a user reaches; the CDN decides where content is stored. Interviewers often ask how DNS and CDN differ from a load balancer.
slides.lead:
Load balancing spreads traffic within one location.
DNS-based routing and content delivery solve the same problem at internet scale, across regions and distant users

points.text: DNS-based routing returns different endpoint addresses based on a policy like location, latency or health
DNS failover swaps a failed address for a healthy one, but only after cached DNS answers expire (TTL)

slides.title: Routing And Delivery
slides.notes: Frame this as traffic steering at a wider scale than load balancing. DNS decides which region a user reaches; the CDN decides where content is stored. Interviewers often ask how DNS and CDN differ from a load balancer.

points.text: A Content Delivery Network (CDN) caches copies of content at edge locations close to users
Edges fetch content from the origin on a cache miss
Cache expiry (TTL) and invalidation keep copies up to date

slides.title: Steering By Resolution
slides.notes: Explain that the same name can resolve to different addresses depending on who asks and from where. Use the enquiry-counter analogy before naming the four policy types. Interviewers may ask how this differs from a load balancer: routing happens before any connection opens.
slides.lead:
Domain Name System (DNS) normally returns one fixed address for a name, but DNS-based routing returns different addresses based on policy.
This steers users to a region without the user noticing any choice

slides.title: Steering By Resolution
slides.notes: Explain that the same name can resolve to different addresses depending on who asks and from where. Use the enquiry-counter analogy before naming the four policy types. Interviewers may ask how this differs from a load balancer: routing happens before any connection opens.

points: Geolocation routing: returns the record assigned to the user’s country or continent
Latency-based routing: picks the region that historically responded fastest to the user
Weighted routing splits DNS answers across regions by a configured traffic percentage
Multi-value answer routing: returns several healthy addresses for the client to choose

slides.label: Analogy: a food delivery app
slides.title: Steering By Resolution
slides.notes:
TR analogy: When you order from a restaurant chain on a food delivery app, the app automatically sends your order to the branch nearest to you or the one that is open and least busy, even though you only searched the restaurant’s name. In the same way, DNS-based routing takes one domain name and returns the address of the regional server best suited for each user.

"Explain that the same name can resolve to different addresses depending on who asks and from where. Use the enquiry-counter analogy before naming the four policy types. Interviewers may ask how this differs from a load balancer: routing happens before any connection opens."

slides.title: Health Checked Record Swap
slides.notes: Connect this to load balancer health checks, but note the checked unit here is an entire region, not one server. The TTL trade-off between fast failover and resolver load is a common interview probe; TTL also governs how fast cached answers expire.
slides.lead: Proximity routing alone cannot sense a region is down, so DNS failover adds continuous health checks that stop including a failed address in new DNS answers

slides.title: Health Checked Record Swap
slides.notes: Connect this to load balancer health checks, but note the checked unit here is an entire region, not one server. The TTL trade-off between fast failover and resolver load is a common interview probe; TTL also governs how fast cached answers expire.

points.text: Route 53 failover routing sends traffic to a primary record, switching to a secondary if it fails
A record failing consecutive checks is marked down and removed from DNS answers
Failover completes after detection plus TTL expiry of cached answers
Lower TTL values speed up failover but raise resolver query load

slides.title: Content Near Users
slides.notes: Define cache hit and miss here, since the next slide builds on both. Name CloudFront as the AWS CDN. A common interview question is why a CDN helps even when the app runs in one region: distance and origin offload.
slides.lead: A CDN keeps copies of content on servers called edge locations, placed close to users, so most requests are answered nearby instead of at a distant origin server

slides.title: Content Near Users
slides.notes: Define cache hit and miss here, since the next slide builds on both. Name CloudFront as the AWS CDN. A common interview question is why a CDN helps even when the app runs in one region: distance and origin offload.

points.text: Edge location: a cache server near users
A cache hit means it already holds the content and replies at once
Cache miss: the edge lacks the content, fetches it from the origin and keeps a copy for the next user
Serving from the edge cuts delay for distant users and shields the origin from repeated requests
Static files such as images, style sheets and scripts cache well; personalised pages cache poorly

slides.label: Analogy: a neighbourhood shop
slides.title: Content Near Users
slides.notes:
TR analogy: “A neighbourhood shop stocks popular items so customers need not travel to a distant factory every time — just as an edge location holds popular content and only the first request travels to the origin.”

“Define cache hit and miss here, since the next slide builds on both. Name CloudFront as the AWS CDN. A common interview question is why a CDN helps even when the app runs in one region: distance and origin offload.”

slides.title: Refreshing Edge Content
slides.notes: Build on the known cache hit/miss idea, noting the miss path is called an origin pull. Explain TTL as the timer deciding when a cached copy turns stale. Exams often ask why static files get long TTLs and dynamic pages do not.
slides.lead: An edge server must decide if its cached copy is still fresh, or stale enough to fetch again from the origin, the authoritative content server

points.text: A cache miss triggers an origin pull, fetching the object fresh
Time to Live (TTL), set via a cache-control header, decides how long an edge copy stays valid
A conditional request confirms a cached copy is still fresh without re-downloading it
Static assets get long TTLs; frequently changing pages get short or no caching

slides.title: Forcing Fresh Content
slides.notes: Present purge and versioning as two answers to the same problem: stale content after an update. The versioned-URL trick is a favourite interview question since it needs no purge call. Note that aggressive purging pushes traffic back onto the origin.
slides.lead:
Waiting for a TTL to expire can leave stale content live for minutes or hours.
Cache invalidation lets an operator remove or bypass it immediately

slides.title: Forcing Fresh Content
slides.notes: Present purge and versioning as two answers to the same problem: stale content after an update. The versioned-URL trick is a favourite interview question since it needs no purge call. Note that aggressive purging pushes traffic back onto the origin.

points.text: Purge invalidation removes an object from every edge before TTL expiry
CloudFront calls this an invalidation request
Versioned URLs attach a new filename or query string, skipping old cached files
A single invalidation request can target one path or an entire cache
Over-invalidating increases origin load since every edge must re-fetch content

slides.title: Two Routing Layers
slides.notes: Use the table to fix the layer and speed difference; this is a common interview question. DNS failover is slower due to TTL caching, while a load balancer reacts within its health-check interval. Both layers are usually combined, not chosen between.
slides.lead:
DNS routing and a load balancer both redirect traffic from a failed target, but they work at different layers and speeds.
Production systems usually combine both

cells: Geo or latency routing to the nearest region
Application Load Balancer and its target group

slides.title: Two Routing Layers
slides.notes: Use the table to fix the layer and speed difference; this is a common interview question. DNS failover is slower due to TTL caching, while a load balancer reacts within its health-check interval. Both layers are usually combined, not chosen between.
slides.lead:
DNS first sends a user to a healthy region, and a load balancer inside that region spreads requests across healthy servers.
The two layers complement rather than replace each other

props.lead: This exercise builds a small load-balanced web tier: two web servers behind one Application Load Balancer, using the VPC and subnets created earlier

note.text: It creates billable AWS resources, so the Billing dashboard should be checked first, and all resources are deleted right after screenshots are captured

points.text: An Application Load Balancer spans more than one Availability Zone
So the servers it balances across must sit in separate zones for true redundancy

slides.label: Task And Steps

steps.text: Verify the VPC, subnets, and route table against the table above before creating anything new
Add one new subnet in a second zone, plus a load balancer security group and a web server security group

Create a target group and register both web servers as its targets

Test the load balancer, then stop and restart a server to observe health checks

props.title: Wrap-Up Checklist
props.lead: The finished setup is a single load balancer domain name that reaches two interchangeable web servers, each able to fail and recover without any manual rerouting of traffic

props.title: Wrap-Up Checklist
props.lead: This classroom setup enables public addresses on both backend servers to keep access simple; in a production deployment, servers sitting behind an internet-facing load balancer are usually placed in private subnets instead, since the load balancer is the only component that needs to be publicly reachable

props.title: Wrap-Up Checklist
props.lead: Cleanup runs in dependency order: the load balancer is deleted first, then the target group, then the two instances are terminated, then `s6-web-sg`, `s6-alb-sg` and `s6-public-subnet-2`, since each resource is still used by the one deleted before it
